title: A House for Mouse
subtitle: A little mouse looks for a cosy place to sleep
credit: Originally published by Book Dash, created by Michele Fry, Amy Uzzell (now Richards) and Jennifer Jacobs, under CC BY 4.0. For Bedtime Bookshelf: new vector artwork and animation; the original wordless fireplace page is grouped into the adjacent scene; original story text preserved and four conversation questions added.

pages.text: Mouse was looking for a new house.
pages.alt: A scarf-wearing grey mouse follows a winding garden path towards a golden cottage.

pages.text: This looks like a nice house.
pages.alt: Mouse pauses on the welcome mat and lifts its nose towards the open green door.

pages.text:
“You can come and sleep with me,” said Puppy.

“Thank you,” said Mouse.
pages.alt: A friendly charcoal puppy wags its tail in a woven basket as Mouse listens.

pages.text: That night, Mouse’s dreams were bouncy and muddy.
pages.alt: In a moonlit dream, Mouse bounces above a muddy puddle while Puppy watches.

pages.text:
“You can come and sleep with me,” said Parrot.

“Thank you,” said Mouse.
pages.alt: A red-headed green parrot opens its wing on a wooden perch; Mouse looks up.

pages.text: That night, Mouse’s dreams were noisy and wild.
pages.alt: Mouse dreams beneath sweeping forest leaves while a parrot calls from a branch.

pages.text:
“You can come and sleep with me,” said Fish.

“Thank you,” said Mouse.
pages.alt: A golden fish swims in its glass bowl on a wooden table as Mouse watches.

pages.text: That night, Mouse’s dreams were cold and wet.
pages.alt: Mouse dreams on an underwater cushion amid tall reeds, goldfish and bubbles.

pages.text: Mouse needed somewhere warm and dry.
pages.alt: Mouse finds a cushioned chair beside a glowing fireplace and warm wooden floor.

pages.text: Mouse found a bookshelf nearby.
pages.alt: Between tall books, Mouse discovers a soft folded blanket in a cosy bookshelf nook.

pages.text: That night, Mouse had warm and cosy dreams.
pages.alt: Mouse sleeps peacefully under a patchwork quilt in the golden light of the bookshelf nook.

questions.q: Who first invited Mouse to come and sleep?
questions.a: Puppy invited Mouse first.

questions.q: Where did Mouse finally find a cosy place to sleep?
questions.a: On a bookshelf nearby.

questions.q: How might Mouse feel in the warm bookshelf bed?
questions.a: Mouse might feel comfortable, safe or happy. Other feelings your child notices are welcome.

questions.q: What makes your own bed feel cosy?
questions.a: There is no wrong answer. Listen and invite your child to tell you more.

title: Big Bear, Little Mouse
subtitle: Two friends make a place to play
credit: Original story and vector illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf with AI assistance. For playful shared reading; not an assessment or certified curriculum.

pages.text: Bear and Mouse were making a play space, with different things for them to share.
pages.alt: Bear and Mouse bring buckets and a cart to an empty garden play space.

pages.text: A big ball and a small ball rolled onto the grass. Both were fun to play with.
pages.alt: Two matching red balls differ clearly in size; Bear watches and Mouse stands beside them.

pages.text: Bear built a tall tower. Mouse built a short tower beside it.
pages.alt: A tall tower of six blue blocks and a short tower of two blue blocks stand on the same ground.

pages.text: One flowerpot was near Mouse. One flowerpot was far from Mouse. He waved to Bear by the far pot.
pages.alt: Mouse stands next to the near flowerpot in the foreground; a second flowerpot and Bear are far across the garden.

pages.text: One bucket was full of sand. One bucket was empty, ready for a turn.
pages.alt: Two equal blue buckets show a full sandy opening and a dark empty interior.

pages.text: One cart rolled fast. The other rolled slowly. Bear and Mouse watched them go.
pages.alt: Two matching carts travel in separate lanes, one fast and one slow, with Bear and Mouse watching nearby.

pages.text: They parked the carts near the towers. There was room for big and small things in their play space.
pages.alt: Big and small balls, tall and short towers and two carts fill the completed play area.

pages.text: “Let’s play together,” said little Mouse. “Yes!” said big Bear.
pages.alt: Bear and Mouse sit together beside a ball in their shared garden.

questions.q: Which tower had more blocks?
questions.a: The tall tower had more blocks.

questions.q: What was in the full bucket?
questions.a: Sand was in the full bucket.

questions.q: How might Mouse feel when Bear agrees to play?
questions.a: There can be different feelings. Listen to the feeling your child notices and why.

questions.q: What big and small things could you play with?
questions.a: Any answer is welcome. Invite your child to tell you more.

title: A Day of Feelings
subtitle: Bear finds words for a changing day
credit: Original story and vector illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf with AI assistance. For playful shared reading; not an assessment or certified curriculum.

pages.text: Bear came to play with Mouse. Who knew what the day would bring?
pages.alt: Bear arrives in the playroom with Mouse and a blue bucket.

pages.text: “I feel happy,” said Bear. Mouse had saved some blocks for him.
pages.alt: Bear smiles beside Mouse and a neat tower of colourful blocks.

pages.text: The tower fell. “I feel sad,” said Bear. Mouse sat with him.
pages.alt: Bear has a downturned mouth and a tear beside fallen blocks; Mouse stays nearby.

pages.text: The blocks would not balance. “I feel angry!” Bear put them down and took a slow breath.
pages.alt: Bear’s eyebrows angle inward and his mouth is tight; the blocks rest safely on the floor.

pages.text: “I feel worried it will fall again,” said Bear. “Can you help me?”
pages.alt: Bear’s raised inner eyebrows and wavy mouth accompany his request for help; Mouse stands by the fallen blocks.

pages.text: Together, they made a wide base. “I feel excited to try!” said Bear.
pages.alt: Bear has an open joyful mouth and raised eyebrows; a wide base supports their rebuilt tower.

pages.text: The tower stood. Bear rested beside Mouse. “Now I feel calm.”
pages.alt: Bear rests with softly closed eyes and a small relaxed smile beside Mouse and the standing tower.

pages.text: “My feelings came and went,” said Bear. “And I could tell you about them.” Mouse stayed close.
pages.alt: Bear and Mouse sit close together on the rug, with the finished tower beside them.

questions.q: What happened to Bear’s first tower?
questions.a: The tower fell.

questions.q: Who helped Bear try again?
questions.a: Mouse helped Bear.

questions.q: How might Bear feel when Mouse stays close?
questions.a: There can be different feelings. Listen to the feeling your child notices and why.

questions.q: Who can you talk to about your feelings?
questions.a: Any answer is welcome. Invite your child to tell you more.

title: The Little Shape Builders
subtitle: A playhouse made from friendly shapes
credit: Original story and vector illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf with AI assistance. For playful shared reading; not an assessment or certified curriculum.

pages.text: Mouse and Rabbit wanted a playhouse. A pile of shapes was a good place to start.
pages.alt: Mouse and Rabbit stand beside four large building shapes in a garden.

pages.text: “A circle for a round window!” said Mouse. The circle had no corners.
pages.alt: A large circular window sits on a workbench, with Mouse beside it.

pages.text: Rabbit chose a square window. It had four equal sides.
pages.alt: One square with four equal straight sides rests beside Rabbit.

pages.text: A triangle made a pointed roof. “Three sides!” said Mouse.
pages.alt: A large triangular roof with three straight sides rests above the unfinished walls.

pages.text: The rectangle became a door. Now the friends could go in.
pages.alt: A tall rectangular blue door has two long sides and two short sides.

pages.text: Mouse matched the circle to the round opening. Rabbit matched the square to the square opening.
pages.alt: Circle and square windows match outlined openings on the playhouse.

pages.text: Circle, square, triangle, rectangle. Together, the shapes made their playhouse!
pages.alt: The completed playhouse combines a triangle roof, square and circular windows, and a rectangle door.

pages.text: The friends opened the door. Inside, there was room for a story.
pages.alt: Mouse waves outside the finished playhouse while Rabbit waits beside it with a book.

questions.q: Which shape made the roof?
questions.a: A triangle made the roof.

questions.q: How many equal sides did the square have?
questions.a: It had four equal sides.

questions.q: How might the friends feel when their playhouse is ready?
questions.a: There can be different feelings. Listen to the feeling your child notices and why.

questions.q: What shape can you find near you?
questions.a: Any answer is welcome. Invite your child to tell you more.

title: Mouse’s Counting Picnic
subtitle: One, two, three — enough to share
credit: Original story and vector illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf with AI assistance. For playful shared reading; not an assessment or certified curriculum.

pages.text: Mouse invited the friends to a picnic. “I’ll count as I pack, so there is plenty to share.”
pages.alt: Mouse stands beside a picnic basket and an empty quilt, ready to pack for friends.

pages.text: One apple to slice and share. Mouse began with 1.
pages.alt: Numeral 1 and exactly 1 separate apples on the packing mat. Mouse counts beside them.

pages.text: 2 cups for pouring water. Mouse touched each cup once.
pages.alt: Numeral 2 and exactly 2 separate cups on the packing mat. Mouse counts beside them.

pages.text: 3 sandwiches for the plate. Mouse counted, “One, two, three.”
pages.alt: Numeral 3 and exactly 3 separate sandwiches on the packing mat. Mouse counts beside them.

pages.text: 4 carrots for a crunchy snack. Rabbit would be pleased.
pages.alt: Numeral 4 and exactly 4 separate carrots on the packing mat. Mouse counts beside them.

pages.text: 5 napkins to wipe sticky paws. Mouse laid them in a row.
pages.alt: Numeral 5 and exactly 5 separate napkins on the packing mat. Mouse counts beside them.

pages.text: 6 spoons for the picnic basket. Mouse counted each one as it went in.
pages.alt: Numeral 6 and exactly 6 separate spoons on the packing mat. Mouse counts beside them.

pages.text: 7 oranges to share with friends. The picnic was growing!
pages.alt: Numeral 7 and exactly 7 separate oranges on the packing mat. Mouse counts beside them.

pages.text: 8 strawberries, bright and red. Mouse checked the count again.
pages.alt: Numeral 8 and exactly 8 separate strawberries on the packing mat. Mouse counts beside them.

pages.text: 9 leaves to decorate the quilt. Mouse left space between them.
pages.alt: Numeral 9 and exactly 9 separate leaves on the packing mat. Mouse counts beside them.

pages.text: 10 flowers for the picnic table. “Everything is ready!” said Mouse.
pages.alt: Numeral 10 and exactly 10 separate flowers on the packing mat. Mouse counts beside them.

pages.text: The friends gathered on the quilt. “Counting helped me get ready,” said Mouse. “Now we can share!”
pages.alt: Mouse, Pip, Rabbit and Bear gather around the picnic quilt with packed food to share.

questions.q: How many apples did Mouse pack?
questions.a: Mouse packed one apple to slice and share.

questions.q: What did Mouse count ten of?
questions.a: Mouse counted ten flowers.

questions.q: How might Mouse feel when the friends arrive?
questions.a: Mouse might feel happy or excited to share. Other ideas are welcome.

questions.q: What would you like to bring to a picnic?
questions.a: Any picnic idea is welcome. You could count a few real objects together.

title: The Pattern Parade
subtitle: What comes next in our celebration?
credit: Original story and vector illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf with AI assistance. For playful shared reading; not an assessment or certified curriculum.

pages.text: The friends were planning a parade. Mouse had an idea: repeating patterns for the decorations.
pages.alt: Mouse and Rabbit prepare a parade arch with an undecorated ribbon and two blue buckets.

pages.text: Red, blue, red, blue. Mouse made a row of round badges.
pages.alt: A left-to-right pattern: red circle, blue circle, red circle, blue circle. Mouse watches without moving the sequence.

pages.text: Yellow, green, yellow, green. Rabbit made another repeating row.
pages.alt: A left-to-right pattern: yellow square, green square, yellow square, green square. Mouse watches without moving the sequence.

pages.text: Circle, triangle, circle, triangle. This pattern changed shape, not colour.
pages.alt: A left-to-right pattern: blue circle, blue triangle, blue circle, blue triangle. Mouse watches without moving the sequence.

pages.text: Red, red, blue. Red, red, blue. Bear tried a longer repeating bit.
pages.alt: A left-to-right pattern: red circle, red circle, blue circle, red circle, red circle, blue circle. Mouse watches without moving the sequence.

pages.text: Yellow, yellow, green. Yellow, yellow, green. The next row was ready too.
pages.alt: A left-to-right pattern: yellow triangle, yellow triangle, green triangle, yellow triangle, yellow triangle, green triangle. Mouse watches without moving the sequence.

pages.text: Red, blue, red, blue, red… One badge was missing. What could come next?
pages.alt: A left-to-right pattern: red circle, blue circle, red circle, blue circle, red circle. Mouse watches without moving the sequence.

pages.text: A blue badge! The pattern was complete. The friends marched past their colourful rows.
pages.alt: The completed red-blue pattern shows six stationary badges above Mouse, Rabbit and Bear in the parade.

questions.q: What came after red in Mouse’s first row?
questions.a: Blue came after red.

questions.q: Which badge filled the empty place?
questions.a: A blue badge filled the empty place.

questions.q: How might the friends feel when the parade is ready?
questions.a: There can be different feelings. Listen to the feeling your child notices and why.

questions.q: What repeating pattern would you make?
questions.a: Any answer is welcome. Invite your child to tell you more.

title: Pip Finds a Friend
subtitle: An original sample about a small act of kindness
credit: Original sample story and SVG illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf. Reconstructed from the project plan; this is not a Book Dash title or the missing prototype artwork.

pages.text: Pip is a little owl. Pip lives in a big green tree.
pages.alt: Pip, a small brown owl, sits on a branch of a green tree beneath a crescent moon.

pages.text: One evening, Pip heard a sound. “Sniff, sniff.” Who was crying?
pages.alt: Pip looks down from the tree at Rabbit, who is crying in the grass.

pages.text: It was Rabbit. “I lost my red ball,” said Rabbit. Rabbit felt very sad.
pages.alt: Rabbit has a tear on one cheek while Pip listens beside a bush.

pages.text: “I will help you look,” said Pip. They looked beside the flowers. No ball!
pages.alt: Pip and Rabbit look beside three yellow flowers. The ball is not there.

pages.text: They looked behind a bush. No ball there, either. Pip looked up.
pages.alt: Pip and Rabbit look around a leafy green bush. The ball is not there.

pages.text: “There it is!” said Pip. The red ball was up in the tree. Pip flew up to get it.
pages.alt: A red ball rests on a high branch. Pip flies toward it while Rabbit waits below.

pages.text: Pip gave the ball to Rabbit. “Thank you, Pip!” said Rabbit. Now Pip had a new friend.
pages.alt: Pip and a smiling Rabbit stand together with the red ball between them.

pages.text: The friends rested under the moon. Rabbit kept the red ball close. “Goodnight, friend,” whispered Pip.
pages.alt: Pip closes his eyes on the tree branch. Rabbit rests below beside the red ball in the moonlight.

questions.q: What did Rabbit lose?
questions.a: A red ball.

questions.q: Where did Pip find the ball?
questions.a: Up in the tree.

questions.q: How did Rabbit feel when the ball was lost?
questions.a: Sad. Rabbit was crying because the ball was lost.

questions.q: Have you ever lost a toy?
questions.a: There is no wrong answer. You could ask who helped your child look.

title: Pip’s Alphabet Adventure
subtitle: An A-to-Z party of things and pictures
credit: Original story and vector illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf with AI assistance. For playful shared reading; not an assessment or certified curriculum.

pages.text: Pip wanted an alphabet party. “Let’s find a thing or a picture for every letter!”
pages.alt: Pip the owl and Mouse prepare an empty display board for their alphabet party.

pages.text: A a — apple. Pip found an apple for the feast.
pages.alt: A a and apple on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: B b — ball. Mouse rolled a ball for their games.
pages.alt: B b and ball on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object, with Mouse nearby.

pages.text: C c — cup. Pip chose a cup for a thirsty guest.
pages.alt: C c and cup on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: D d — drum. A drum would call everyone together.
pages.alt: D d and drum on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: E e — egg. Pip drew an egg on a little card.
pages.alt: E e and egg on a large card and plaque. Pip shows a drawn picture.

pages.text: F f — fish. By the pond, Pip drew a fish.
pages.alt: F f and fish on a large card and plaque. Pip shows a drawn picture.

pages.text: G g — gift. Mouse wrapped a gift for the guests.
pages.alt: G g and gift on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object, with Mouse nearby.

pages.text: H h — hat. Pip borrowed a sunny yellow hat.
pages.alt: H h and hat on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: I i — insect. An insect landed nearby. Pip drew its six legs.
pages.alt: I i and insect on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: J j — jug. A jug would hold cool water.
pages.alt: J j and jug on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: K k — kite. Pip chose a kite for the breezy field.
pages.alt: K k and kite on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: L l — leaf. A leaf would look lovely on the party table.
pages.alt: L l and leaf on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: M m — moon. Pip made a moon picture for the evening.
pages.alt: M m and moon on a large card and plaque. Pip shows a drawn picture.

pages.text: N n — nest. Pip drew a nest and left the real one safe.
pages.alt: N n and nest on a large card and plaque. Pip shows a drawn picture.

pages.text: O o — orange. An orange joined the picnic food.
pages.alt: O o and orange on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: P p — paintbrush. A paintbrush helped Pip finish the pictures.
pages.alt: P p and paintbrush on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: Q q — quilt. Mouse brought a quilt for everyone to sit on.
pages.alt: Q q and quilt on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object, with Mouse nearby.

pages.text: R r — rabbit. Rabbit came along to help.
pages.alt: R r and rabbit on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: S s — sock. A clean sock became a silly puppet.
pages.alt: S s and sock on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: T t — teddy. Mouse brought a teddy to join the fun.
pages.alt: T t and teddy on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object, with Mouse nearby.

pages.text: U u — umbrella. An umbrella would give a patch of shade.
pages.alt: U u and umbrella on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: V v — vase. Pip found a vase for the table.
pages.alt: V v and vase on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: W w — wagon. A wagon carried the party things.
pages.alt: W w and wagon on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: X x — x-ray. Mouse brought an x-ray picture showing bones.
pages.alt: X x and x-ray on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object, with Mouse nearby.

pages.text: Y y — yarn. Yarn tied the picture cards together.
pages.alt: Y y and yarn on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: Z z — zip. Pip closed the bag with its zip.
pages.alt: Z z and zip on a large card and plaque. Pip stands beside the learning object.

pages.text: The alphabet party was ready, from A to Z. “We can visit our favourite letters again,” said Pip.
pages.alt: Pip, Mouse and Rabbit celebrate under alphabet bunting, with a quilt, food and the picture cards.

questions.q: What was Pip getting ready for?
questions.a: An alphabet party.

questions.q: What carried the party things?
questions.a: A wagon carried the party things.

questions.q: How might Pip feel when the party is ready?
questions.a: Pip might feel happy, proud or excited. Other ideas are welcome.

questions.q: Which thing or picture would you bring to an alphabet party?
questions.a: Any idea is welcome. You can name its first letter together if you like.

title: Pip’s Planet Journey
subtitle: An imaginary trip past eight real planets
credit: Original story and vector illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf with AI assistance. For playful shared reading; not an assessment or certified curriculum.

pages.text: Pip imagines a trip past eight planets. The Sun is a star, and the Moon is not a planet.
pages.alt: Pip imagines a space journey beside an empty cardboard rocket. A thought cloud names the Sun as a star and the Moon as not a planet.

pages.text: Mercury is the smallest planet. Pip starts close to the Sun.
pages.alt: Pip in a cardboard rocket beside Mercury, 1 from the Sun. Its features are shown with a shaded side; a fixed strip marks its order. Not to scale.

pages.text: Venus is the hottest planet. Pip looks from far away.
pages.alt: Pip in a cardboard rocket beside Venus, 2 from the Sun. Its features are shown with a shaded side; a fixed strip marks its order. Not to scale.

pages.text: Earth has oceans of water. Pip waves to home.
pages.alt: Pip in a cardboard rocket beside Earth, 3 from the Sun. Its features are shown with a shaded side; a fixed strip marks its order. Not to scale.

pages.text: Mars looks red from far away. Pip spots the dusty planet.
pages.alt: Pip in a cardboard rocket beside Mars, 4 from the Sun. Its features are shown with a shaded side; a fixed strip marks its order. Not to scale.

pages.text: Jupiter is the biggest planet. Pip gazes at the giant.
pages.alt: Pip in a cardboard rocket beside Jupiter, 5 from the Sun. Its features are shown with a shaded side; a fixed strip marks its order. Not to scale.

pages.text: Saturn has rings of ice and rock. Pip draws a ring in the air.
pages.alt: Pip in a cardboard rocket beside Saturn, 6 from the Sun. Its features are shown with a shaded side; a fixed strip marks its order. Not to scale.

pages.text: Uranus spins on its side. Pip tilts his head.
pages.alt: Pip in a cardboard rocket beside Uranus, 7 from the Sun. Its features are shown with a shaded side; a fixed strip marks its order. Not to scale.

pages.text: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun. Pip is ready to go home.
pages.alt: Pip in a cardboard rocket beside Neptune, 8 from the Sun. Its features are shown with a shaded side; a fixed strip marks its order. Not to scale.

pages.text: Pip lands on his soft rug. “Hello, Earth. It is good to be home!”
pages.alt: Pip stands at home on a soft rug beside an empty cardboard rocket and a moonlit window.

questions.q: Which planet is the biggest?
questions.a: Jupiter is the biggest planet.

questions.q: Which planet has rings of ice and rock?
questions.a: Saturn has rings of ice and rock.

questions.q: How does Pip feel about coming home?
questions.a: Pip says he is glad to be home.

questions.q: Which planet would you draw?
questions.a: Choose any planet, or imagine a picture together.

title: Rabbit’s Rainbow Garden
subtitle: Seven colours make a place to share
credit: Original story and vector illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf with AI assistance. For playful shared reading; not an assessment or certified curriculum.

pages.text: Rabbit dreams of a garden full of colours. Where will she find them?
pages.alt: Rabbit stands by empty garden beds with a watering can while a butterfly visits.

pages.text: Red flowers! Rabbit plants them by the gate.
pages.alt: Rabbit explores red flowers in a softly coloured garden. The word red is on a cream plaque.

pages.text: Orange carrots! Rabbit gives them a drink.
pages.alt: Rabbit explores orange carrots in a softly coloured garden. The word orange is on a cream plaque.

pages.text: Yellow sunflowers! They reach up to the sun.
pages.alt: Rabbit explores yellow flowers in a softly coloured garden. The word yellow is on a cream plaque.

pages.text: Green leaves! They make a cool little nook.
pages.alt: Rabbit explores green leaves in a softly coloured garden. The word green is on a cream plaque.

pages.text: Blue flowers! Mouse brings some for the path.
pages.alt: Rabbit explores blue flowers in a softly coloured garden. The word blue is on a cream plaque.

pages.text: Purple plums! Rabbit finds them on the tree.
pages.alt: Rabbit explores purple plums on the tree in a softly coloured garden. The word purple is on a cream plaque.

pages.text: Pink flowers! A soft pink corner, just for Rabbit’s garden.
pages.alt: Rabbit explores pink flowers in a softly coloured garden. The word pink is on a cream plaque.

pages.text: Rabbit matches each flower to a colour pot. Can you find the blue pair?
pages.alt: Seven flowers line up over matching red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple and pink pots. Rabbit watches.

pages.text: The colour garden is ready. Rabbit and Mouse share a rainbow of garden colours!
pages.alt: Rabbit and Mouse sit together among red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple and pink garden flowers; no sky rainbow is shown.

questions.q: What colour are the carrots?
questions.a: The carrots are orange.

questions.q: Who brings blue flowers?
questions.a: Mouse brings blue flowers.

questions.q: How might Rabbit feel when the garden is ready?
questions.a: She might feel proud, glad or peaceful. Other ideas are welcome.

questions.q: Which garden colour would you choose?
questions.a: Any colour is welcome; you can point to one.

title: Sleepy Mr Sloth
subtitle: A sleepy climb to the perfect branch
credit: Originally published by Book Dash under a Creative Commons CC BY 4.0 licence. This book can be read for free on www.bookdash.org and was created by Paul Kennedy (writer), Graham Paterson (illustrator), Nick Mulgrew (designer) and Arthur Attwell (editor). For Bedtime Bookshelf, illustrations were converted to WebP, selected parts of each illustration were separated and animated with repaired backgrounds, the original text was laid out separately, and four conversation questions were added.

pages.text:
One day, Mr Sloth came to visit. He said:

I’m sleepy! I need a good branch for a bed!
pages.alt: Mr Sloth is sleepy and yawning.

pages.text:
I’m quite good at climbing. I know how to swing.

But sleeping’s my favourite, favourite thing!
pages.alt: Mr Sloth starts climbing the tree.

pages.text:
This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here.

And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?
pages.alt: Mr Sloth spots a branch. Is that a big ear nearby?

pages.text:
Oh no, Mr Sloth! A giraffe’s eating there!

He might think you’re lunch and start nibbling your hair!
pages.alt: A giraffe bites Mr Sloth by mistake!

pages.text:
This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here.

And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?
pages.alt: Mr Sloth spots a branch. There are a few bees flying around.

pages.text:
Oh no, Mr Sloth! There’s a beehive right there!

You’ll never get sleep with those bees everywhere!
pages.alt: Bees fly out of a beehive around Mr Sloth!

pages.text:
This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here.

And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?
pages.alt: Mr Sloth spots a branch. There is a tail nearby.

pages.text:
Oh no, Mr Sloth, that’s a snake over there!

Not a branch! Poor old snake. You gave him quite a scare.
pages.alt: Mr Sloth grabs snake by mistake!

pages.text:
This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here.

And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?
pages.alt: Mr Sloth spots a branch. There are feet nearby.

pages.text:
Oh no, Mr Sloth! There’s a bird squawking there!

You’ll never get sleep with that noise in the air!
pages.alt: A hadeda is squawking loudly there!

pages.text:
Try climb one more branch, Mr Sloth! they all said.

And that branch was just the right one for his bed.
pages.alt: Mr Sloth climbs to the top of the tree and smiles.

pages.text:
The bird and the snake, the giraffe and each bee

were happy to have Mr Sloth in their tree.
pages.alt: Mr Sloth and the animals are all sleeping nicely in the tree together.

questions.q: What did Mr Sloth want to do?
questions.a: Sleep! He wanted a good branch for a bed.

questions.q: Who made a loud squawking noise?
questions.a: The bird. It was too noisy for Mr Sloth to sleep there.

questions.q: How did the animals feel at the end?
questions.a: Happy to have Mr Sloth in their tree. Other feelings your child notices are welcome, too.

questions.q: Where do you like to sleep?
questions.a: There is no wrong answer. Listen, then invite your child to tell you more.

title: The Weather Window
subtitle: Mouse and Pip peek at faraway skies
credit: Original story and vector illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf with AI assistance. For playful shared reading; not an assessment or certified curriculum.

pages.text: Mouse finds a pretend travel window. “Let’s look at weather in faraway places!”
pages.alt: Mouse and Pip face a golden pretend window with a winding path through green hills.

pages.text: A sunny place! Mouse sees bright light on the grass.
pages.alt: Through their pretend travel window Mouse and Pip see a sunny place: sunlight over grass and a butterfly.

pages.text: A rainy place! Drops splash into a puddle.
pages.alt: Through their pretend travel window Mouse and Pip see a rainy place: rain falling into a puddle.

pages.text: A windy place! The wind lifts a little kite.
pages.alt: Through their pretend travel window Mouse and Pip see a windy place: a kite lifted beside a bending tree.

pages.text: A cloudy place! Soft clouds cover much of the sky.
pages.alt: Through their pretend travel window Mouse and Pip see a cloudy place: large clouds covering much of the sky.

pages.text: A snowy place! White flakes settle on the ground.
pages.alt: Through their pretend travel window Mouse and Pip see a snowy place: snowflakes over white ground and fir trees.

pages.text: A sun hat, rain boots, a warm coat. “We choose for the weather,” says Mouse.
pages.alt: Mouse chooses clothes on three labelled hooks: sun hat for sunny weather, rain boots for rainy weather, warm coat for cold snowy weather.

pages.text: They close the pretend window and look outside. “What is the weather like here?” asks Mouse.
pages.alt: Mouse and Pip sit by their real small window looking at pale sky and a cloud, with coat, boots and hat ready nearby.

questions.q: What lifts the kite?
questions.a: The wind lifts the kite.

questions.q: What does Mouse choose for rainy weather?
questions.a: Mouse chooses rain boots.

questions.q: How might Mouse feel looking through the pretend window?
questions.a: Mouse might feel curious, excited or surprised. Other ideas are welcome.

questions.q: What is the weather like where you are?
questions.a: Look together and describe what you notice; no single answer is expected.

title: Where Is Teddy?
subtitle: A hide-and-seek game with Mouse
credit: Original story and vector illustrations created for Bedtime Bookshelf with AI assistance. For playful shared reading; not an assessment or certified curriculum.

pages.text: Rabbit had a game for Mouse. “Close your eyes. I’ll hide Teddy!”
pages.alt: Rabbit holds a small teddy in the cosy room while Mouse closes his eyes.

pages.text: Mouse looked in the box. There was Teddy, in the box!
pages.alt: Teddy sits inside an open box, with the front of the box covering his lower body.

pages.text: Rabbit hid Teddy again. This time, Teddy was on the stool.
pages.alt: The whole teddy sits on the top surface of a low stool.

pages.text: Mouse bent down. Teddy was under the table!
pages.alt: Teddy is fully visible beneath the tabletop, between its four legs.

pages.text: Two round ears peeked out. Teddy was behind the box.
pages.alt: Teddy’s ears and head peek above a solid box that hides his body.

pages.text: Now Teddy was beside the box, where Mouse could see all of him.
pages.alt: The entire teddy sits to the right of the box with a clear gap between them.

pages.text: For the last turn, Rabbit gave a clue. “Look under something with four legs.”
pages.alt: Mouse considers a table with Teddy clearly visible beneath it, and Rabbit watches the search.

pages.text: “Under the table!” Mouse found Teddy and cuddled him close. Now it was Mouse’s turn to hide him.
pages.alt: Mouse cuddles Teddy after finding him beneath the table; Rabbit waits for a new round.

questions.q: Where was Teddy on the first turn?
questions.a: Teddy was in the box.

questions.q: Where was Teddy for the last turn?
questions.a: Teddy was under the table.

questions.q: How might Mouse feel after finding Teddy?
questions.a: There can be different feelings. Listen to the feeling your child notices and why.

questions.q: Where would you hide a toy?
questions.a: Any answer is welcome. Invite your child to tell you more.
